tagline.text: A Davao museum of animal skeletons that tells environmental stories through whale bones

location.label: Location
location.text: San Pedro Extension, Bucana (Barangay 76-A), Davao City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (a good indoor option on rainy days)

children.text: A private animal bone museum in Davao opened in 2012 by American collector Darrell Blatchley. With a guide, you can look at hundreds of skeletons, including whales and dolphins, and think about environmental problems.

D' Bone Collector Museum is a small animal bone museum in the Bucana area on the waterfront side of Davao City. Built on the private collection of American animal collector Darrell Blatchley, it opened in
January 2012
and is still counted among the most unusual indoor attractions in Davao. The exhibit building has three floors, and the bones and skulls of land animals and sea animals are divided by floor.

What sets this place apart from a simple curiosity is its purpose. The museum explains how each animal died, and shows how plastic and other waste dumped in the sea, and pollution made by people, affect wildlife. That is why admission includes a guide who explains the exhibits, and as you walk through you hear animal stories and environmental stories together.
A little more on the history. In 2015 a Davao local outlet reported that the museum started on a site of about
250 m²
with some 150 specimens on
January 27, 2012

. According to a 2014 GMA report, it had passed 20,000 visitors by its second anniversary, and one or two specimens were being added each week. The same report described a policy of not buying native animals, for conservation and legal reasons. It began small, but word of mouth made it an environmental education spot in Davao.

The size of the collection differs from report to report. A 2014 report said more than 500 specimens, a 2015 local outlet said 1,150, and a recent guide mentions more than 700. Rather than the exact count, it is enough to know there are varied specimens gathered from the Philippines and from places such as Canada, Russia, Indonesia and Thailand. The 2014 report presented a sperm whale skeleton about
41 feet
(roughly 12 m) long as the signature exhibit. The museum is not large, so
1 to 1.5 hours

is enough to see it. It is a good stop between other Davao sightseeing, on a rainy day or when you want to escape the heat. It suits families with children and anyone interested in science and natural history.

These are the centerpiece of the museum. In 2015 a local outlet reported that of 83 whale and dolphin species worldwide, 27 occur in the Philippines and 18 in the Davao Gulf, and that the museum had collected 14 of them. You can see for yourself how large and intricate marine mammals are. Because whales and dolphins are so big that you rarely see their bone structure, many visitors say the real size is very different from photos.
A 2014 GMA report presented a sperm whale skeleton about
41 feet

(roughly 12 m) long as the signature exhibit, and an October 2025 visitor account also describes the same 41-foot skeleton on the third floor. The Subangan Museum in Mati has a different sperm whale skeleton (about 16 m), so do not confuse the two.
The second floor displays the bones and skulls of land animals. It is fun to compare how teeth, jaws and bone structure differ with each animal's diet and way of life.
Many visitor accounts say a guide's explanation is included in admission. Visitors say the guide explains each animal's name, where it lives, and even why it died.

The museum explains how human activity has affected wildlife, such as marine animals that swallowed plastic waste. It is a heavy but meaningful theme, and it is often used for environmental education for children. The museum is described as having opened to raise environmental awareness, and a local outlet called it an eco-tourism destination in Davao.

Besides specimens the collector gathered from his teens, the museum is described as holding specimens donated by museums and institutions in Canada, Russia, Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and elsewhere. You can see animals from several regions in one place.

The tour adds stories of whales, dolphins and local wildlife found in the Philippines. Once you know the animals of the Davao Gulf, you will look at beaches and the sea differently on later parts of your trip.
You tour a single three-story building with a guide, so it is hardly tiring. It is fine for seniors and for traveling with children; just allow for moving up and down the stairs between floors.
Arrive at the museum when it opens. Buy your ticket at the entrance and a guide will join you. To avoid busy group times, right after opening is quieter.
Start on the first floor and go up floor by floor while listening to the guide. In the marine animal area, ask the guide first whether photos are allowed in front of the whale and dolphin skeletons.
After the tour, look around at any souvenirs or donation information. Any support is entirely voluntary.
Head back into the city for lunch. Davao is a city with good seafood and fruit.
Continue a city history course by visiting
San Pedro Cathedral, Davao
nearby.
The museum's operating days and hours have changed in the past. Check using its contact details before you leave.
Take a Grab from your hotel to the museum. Leave with time to spare so you arrive around opening time (about 10:00).
After entering, join the guided tour. With the floor-by-floor explanation and the environmental stories, it takes a little over an hour.
Return to the city for lunch and rest briefly at your accommodation.
Visit
San Pedro Cathedral, Davao
If you have time left, rest near your accommodation and plan dinner. The Philippine Eagle Center is a long way away, so a different day is recommended.
The Philippine Eagle Center is far from the city, so it is better to plan it for another day.
There are several direct flights a day from Manila (NAIA) to Francisco Bangoy International Airport, Davao (DVO). The flight takes about
2 hours
There are also flights to Davao from other cities such as Cebu. Check airline schedules and fares at the time of booking.
The easiest way is to enter 'D' Bone Collector Museum' as your destination in the Grab app.
If you take a taxi, ask to go to the corner of Quezon Blvd. and San Pedro St. From there, follow the museum sign into the alley, and visitors report the museum is on the right.
The travel time and fare from the airport to the city vary with traffic, so check locally.
Sources write the address differently, as 76-A Bucana, Talomo District, or Poblacion District. Use the map app coordinates to find it.
Taxis, Grab and jeepneys run in Davao city. It is easier to reach this museum by taxi or Grab than by jeepney.
It is an indoor exhibit, so you can visit all year. Weather hardly matters, but it is especially useful on rainy days.
It is a good substitute when rain spoils your outdoor sightseeing in the city. Sources disagree on operating days (whether it is closed on Sundays) and hours, so check before you go.

During weekends, holidays and school group visits, the exhibit space can get crowded. To hear the guide comfortably, weekday mornings right after opening are recommended. Hours may change during long holidays and school breaks, so check ahead.

Rather than staying near the museum, the usual approach is to book a hotel in central Davao and travel by Grab. The city has everything from budget to high-end hotels. If you only come for the museum, any central hotel makes little difference.
After your visit, we suggest returning to the city to eat. Nothing is confirmed about facilities inside the museum, so bring a little water.

Davao has plenty of restaurants for a couple of meals, and going from the museum to the city center by Grab is the usual way. If you leave the museum around 11:30 when the visit ends, you can partly avoid the lunch rush.
Since a guide is included in admission, listening to the explanation is the main point. If you prepare questions, you will hear more.
There is a notice that children aged 5 and up are charged admission. Check locally for how younger children are treated.
Photo limits and flash use may be restricted to protect the exhibits, so ask the guide first.
It is a narrow indoor space, so aim for right after opening to avoid crowded times.
Before visiting, check operating days and hours by phone or Facebook page. The listed phone number is 0919-624-0744.
Payment methods are unconfirmed, so bring plenty of cash.
You can build a day course by combining it with other Davao sights (the cathedral, the Eagle Center and so on).
Before the tour, tell the guide which animals interest you (whales, birds, reptiles and so on), and they may explain those in more depth. Check locally whether there is a fixed route.
If your Davao stay is short, a half day of the museum in the morning and the city cathedral and a meal in the afternoon is an efficient route.
Check the dates of recent map app reviews and confirm once more by phone or Facebook to avoid a wasted trip.
Fees, hours and exhibits differ between sources and current information is uncertain, so always check right before you visit.
Admission has changed a lot, from ₱50–80 in the past to ₱200–250 in recent visitor accounts. Confirm on site.
Sources differ on operating days, such as closed Sundays or opening on Saturday afternoons.
Specimen counts and descriptions differ by source and period, so do not set your expectations too high.
It sits inside an alley and is hard to find at first. Use a map app and Grab.
Because it is an animal bone exhibit, it may not suit people who dislike odors or a dim atmosphere, or very young children.
As a small private museum, do not expect the facilities and signage of a large national museum. The guide's explanation is the heart of the visit.
A Catholic church that is good for continuing a city history route. It is a short taxi or Grab ride.
A place that protects the Philippine eagle, the national bird. It pairs well with the museum on a wildlife conservation theme. You get there from the city by car.
The city that holds the museum itself. Enjoy city sightseeing and food together.
A resort island reached by boat, good to schedule on a different day after the museum visit.
